title: Benchmark harness: offline vs live script integration
summary: POC scoping focused on how Atlas will supply customer scripts to Redwood's benchmark harness, tradeoffs between offline (replay) vs live streaming load, success criteria (p90 tail latency, 95% availability under peak qps, token cost targets), and a four-week timeline with two benchmark runs and a production-mirroring acceptance test.
topics: Workload sizing and realistic traffic modeling
Customer script integration and adapter changes
Streaming vs non-streaming load tests and fallback behavior
action_items: Marta: share sanitized customer scripts + 2 sample conversation traces (due: 2027-01-13)
Priya: produce harness adapter spec and small example repo (due: 2027-01-11)
Alan: send POC statement of work and pricing worksheet (due: 2027-01-12)
Tom: provide peak QPS and 95th/99th token length distribution CSVs (due: 2027-01-14)
Diego: run initial dry-run with Atlas scripts and share trimmed logs (due: 2027-01-20)
next_steps: Redwood to run baseline offline replay within 48-72 hours after scripts received
Plan full streaming stress run in week 3 of POC
Customer to nominate security contact for VPC/Private deployment questions
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-09 15:30 UTC
Duration: 65 minutes
Recording: (internal link)

---

00:00 Alan Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to do a quick kickoff for the benchmark integration. i know we have the high level poc fl ow but want to align on how your scripts fit into our harness.
00:12 Marta Ruiz: thanks alan yeah, we rearranged some things on our side, we have the customer interactions exported from our production gateway, they include a fair amount of metadata and also a few long multimodal prompts, not images just long context.
00:25 Priya Kapoor: awesome, can you remind us roughly peak qps and typical seq lengths? that helps decide streaming vs non-streaming.
00:33 Tom Brooks: yeah peak is about 450 qps across our fleet right now, tho 90% of traffic is smaller, median tokens per request is 45, 95th is about 380 tokens. we do have a small subset of long sessions that go 1k+ tokens.
00:49 Alan Chen: ok that's useful, so initial plan: we do two main benchmark modes: offline replay (you hand us scripts/traces) and live streaming stress (we emulate sockets and streaming). for acceptance we usually ask to meet p90 latency target and an availability / error budget.
01:02 Sarah Li: what's the difference operationally? i mean is streaming much harder? our infra team wants to know if we need to open ports or change our traffic mirror.
01:12 Priya Kapoor: good q. streaming is marginally more complex — we need to emulate client-side chunking and keep open bidi streams to the runtime. offline replay is basically sequence of full requests replayed at QPS, it's easier to reason about because there's no partial reply state. but streaming uncovers tail latency and cold-start behaviors that offline may miss.
01:33 Marta Ruiz: and our concern is that some of our clients rely on prefix caching across turns so we want the harness to preserve conversation boundaries and kv cache semantics, if possible.
01:42 Diego Alvarez: can you describe the conversation boundary format in your traces? is it single file per user, are there timestamps?
01:49 Marta Ruiz: we have per-session JSONL, each event has a timestamp and an event_type (user_agent, system_prompt, user_message). we can sanitize PD and deliver stripped traces.
01:58 Alan Chen: perfect that's ideal. for the harness adapter we'll need a mapping doc: which fields map to prompt, which map to metadata, any special markers for streaming mid-turn edits.
02:09 Tom Brooks: we'll put together a mapping doc. also on security: do you need access to our VPC or can we just ship sanitized offline traces?
02:18 Priya Kapoor: offline traces are sufficient for the first baseline run. if later we do a private deployment or on-prem, we'll discuss VPC peering or VPN. for hosted runs we never ingest PII — we ask for sanitized data.
02:30 Sarah Li: acceptance criteria, concretely? what numbers do you want us to hit?
02:36 Alan Chen: here's a starting proposal: p90 < 300 ms for short requests (< 128 tokens) under nominal load (60% peak), 95% availability (errors <5%) under peak 450 qps, and cost-per-1k-tokens under an agreed threshold (we'll include that in the SOW). those are negotiable.
03:02 Marta Ruiz: p90 300ms seems optimistic given our current in-house latency, but it's fine for a target. can you also report tail beyond 99th, i.e. 99.9? we have some SLO requirements.
03:14 Priya Kapoor: yes we'll produce full percentile curves: p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 and cold-start distributions. also breakdown by model variant and quantization profile.
03:26 Tom Brooks: about models — are you running one model family or multiple variants in the poc? we'd like to see a smaller, cheaper variant as a fallback.
03:33 Diego Alvarez: good call. we normally test two variants: baseline base-model and a quantized fast variant for cost comparison. fallback routing behavior will be part of a separate test where we simulate a capacity shortage.
03:47 Marta Ruiz: about the harness adapter — do you expect us to rewrite our client code? it'd be expensive.
03:52 Alan Chen: no, we prefer you supply a translation layer: a small adapter script that converts your JSONL events to the harness event format. Priya will share an example repo.
04:00 Priya Kapoor: i can share a 5-file example: adapter.py, README, sample_schema.jsonl, run-harness.sh, and a mini dockerfile. that should be enough for your engs to plug in.
04:11 Tom Brooks: brilliant. is there a performance overhead for adapter vs native?
04:15 Priya Kapoor: negligible for most cases; the adapter runs client-side to construct requests. the only overhead is if you add pre-processing (like heavy tokenization) on the client. we recommend tokenization be consistent with the model tokenizer — we'll provide the tokenizer version.
04:30 Sarah Li: let's talk timeline. we need two full benchmark runs: baseline offline replay and a streaming stress run. how long does each take?
04:37 Alan Chen: baseline dry-run should be quick — once we get sanitized traces and your mapping doc we can run a small offline replay (10-20 minutes of simulated time) within 48-72 hours. full baseline with load shaping to simulate a day's worth of traffic may take up to 48 hours of bench cycles. streaming stress run needs more orchestration and we suggest scheduling a 4-6 hour window in week 3 of the POC.
05:02 Marta Ruiz: ok that aligns. we were planning a 4 week POC window. week 1: adapter + dry-run, week 2: baseline tuning, week 3: streaming stress, week 4: acceptance and handoff. is that realistic?
05:15 Alan Chen: yes that maps to our usual flow, we can compress if you need faster but risks less parity.
05:21 Tom Brooks: for streaming tests we will need to mirror some live traffic. can we use a replay that preserves inter-message timings?
05:28 Priya Kapoor: absolutely — our harness supports time-jittered replay where we reproduce inter-event intervals or compress them for faster stress testing. we also support ramping and sawtooth load shapes.
05:39 Marta Ruiz: in terms of metrics, we want token-level cost, per-route latency, then per-tenant breakdown. can you get token cost broken down by model variant easily?
05:49 Diego Alvarez: yes we produce token accounting and cost estimates for each model/quant profile and request type. we'll attach a cost matrix in the SOW.
05:56 Sarah Li: any regulatory checks? we operate in EU/UK — does that change anything?
06:02 Priya Kapoor: we have private deployment options for EU regions, support KMS integration, SOC 2, and can run in your VPC if needed. for the initial POC with sanitized traces, regional data residency isn't a blocker.
06:15 Tom Brooks: one more thing — our platform uses k v cache semantics across turns; we need to be sure the runtime preserves kv semantics for streaming so that prompts don't drift.
06:25 Priya Kapoor: noted. we'll instrument and validate kv cache hit rates during the streaming run and report any cache-mismatch issues. if we see divergence we'll capture debug dumps for replay.
06:36 Marta Ruiz: perfect. are you able to simulate spotty connectivity? we have clients on flaky mobile networks.
06:42 Diego Alvarez: yes harness can inject network flaps and chunk drops to validate robustness of streaming sessions and fallback to non-streaming. it's an optional test.
06:52 Alan Chen: summary of immediate deliverables: priya adapter spec + example (by 1/11), marta share traces and mapping (by 1/13), alan send SOW and pricing (by 1/12), tom supply traffic distributions (by 1/14). dry-run within 72 hours after receiving traces. schedule checkpoint for 1/21.
07:09 Sarah Li: ok i will loop in our security lead to handle the data sanitization questions and the SREs for the streaming window.
07:16 Marta Ruiz: one question about benchmark fairness — do you allow us to pin model versions and disable autoscaling to measure cold-starts separately?
07:24 Priya Kapoor: yes we support pinning and fixed capacity modes. we'll run both autoscaled and pinned tests to compare cold-start tails.
07:32 Tom Brooks: what about observability hooks — we want token-level traces and structured logs that we can ingest into Splunk.
07:38 Diego Alvarez: we can export logs as JSONL and provide a Splunk ingestion recipe. we'll avoid PII in logs, obviously.
07:45 Alan Chen: any other blockers?
07:48 Marta Ruiz: nothing else from me. thanks everyone.
07:51 Alan Chen: great thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
07:55 End of recording.
